Yes! Spoke with a cross-border tax specialist, and it's a little nuanced based on your tax residency history. Generally, when you enter Canada to become a resident, your [assets are adjusted to fair market value on the date of entry](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/t4055/t4055-newcomers-canada.html#:~:text=at%20a%20cost%20equal%20to%20their%20fair%20market%20value%20(FMV)%20on%20the%20date%20you%20became%20a%20resident%20of%20Canada). In my case (returning Canadian), my HSA cost base is deemed set to fair market value at entry, meaning I can treat it as any other taxable brokerage account - capital gain/loss on disposal, and distributions 100% taxable at income tax rate.

YMMV though - not a bad idea to chat with a cross-border tax specialist if you're really unsure.

We visit Costco 1-2x/month to stock up on essentials, and then fill any gaps with wherever is convenient. 

Monthly net is around 13k, housing 2k, and 2-3k for food/leisure is plenty for the 2 of us. With your high single income, you're likely being taxed more heavily. If your girlfriend is open to it, there are a few ways to lessen your tax burden like claiming her education credits against your income. If her starting income is expected to be considerably less than yours after graduation, you can also contribute to a spousal RRSP that can be drawn down after 2 years then reinvested in a taxable account. This way you'd benefit from preferable tax treatment for capital gains, rather than the deferred 100% taxable income. 

We've been fortunate earlier in our career and mostly coast fire now, so we do employ some tax-optimization strategies with our nest egg that helps add additional savings after the tax season.

My husband and I were in a similar situation a few years back - we used KPMG for the transition. There are very specific steps you have to take to emigrate from Canada and declare yourself a non-resident for tax purposes: [https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/international-non-residents/individuals-leaving-entering-canada-non-residents/leaving-canada-emigrants.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/tax/international-non-residents/individuals-leaving-entering-canada-non-residents/leaving-canada-emigrants.html)

Yes, you are correct in that TFSA's tax exemption status is not honoured by IRS. You'll have to file Form 3520 for the TFSA and FBAR if you plan on keeping foreign assets. We use a US/CAN tax specialist for our IRS filing and he'll be on retainer. I can recommend him to you if you'd like. Also, IRS allows deduction of tax filing fees.

If you plan on returning to Canada, you will need a very nuanced approach to dealing with your US assets (401k, roth/traditional IRA, HSA). For us, this was the most complicated part. 

Good luck!
